title: Back to Back
mood: One narrow street, a wall of doors and shop signs, and a frontline that holds together.

hero.alt: Official art: Layla, long pink twin tails, swings her great white cannon one way while Fanny, short orange hair, cuts with her blade the other way, the two of them back to back.

segs.t: They had held the street for minutes.
All four long-legged Enders lay in front of the gap now, one across another. Everything behind them had to climb the heap and come down into the gap one at a time.
Layla stood at the wall with her cannon dead on her back, counting.
An Ender lifted its arm before it struck. From the lift to the split of its chest plates was always a count of three. She had timed it on the first ones.
Fanny had built the wall the way soldiers without suits had taught her. Across the narrowest place, with one gap. Nobody swung until an Ender swung. When its chest opened, steel went into the core.
The alley thing,
thought Layla. Once she had spied on it from a dark gallery, and then pretended she had never heard of it.
In the gap Guinevere stood with her fists up. Vexana was at her shoulder, the dark staff in her hands.
“The big one,” said Vexana. “It strikes first.”
Vexana knew which one would swing. Layla knew when.
The big one’s arm went up. “Three!” Layla called along the wall. “Two! Now!”
The arm came down. The plates split. Guinevere’s fist went into the core, and the Ender slid back down the heap.
The next one came over too fast. Vexana got the dark staff under its leg and heaved, and it went down the heap on its back.
Along the wall the Shield’s soldiers had their rifles laid across the stack. Their rounds went into a chest only while it stood open. They had begun to fire on Layla’s count. Fanny struck on it too.
Then the Enders found the weak end of the wall.
Where it met a house front, the shop sign slid. A claw came over the top of it.
Layla threw her shoulder against the sign. Above it the Ender reared and lifted its arm at her. Fanny came along the wall at a run.
“Three,” Layla said into the sign. “Two. Now!”
She ducked, her shoulder still in the sign. The arm came down. Its chest plates split, and Fanny’s steel went into the core. The claw tore into the sign above her head.
The Ender fell back off the wall.
Fanny pulled her blade free. “See? You covered me.”
“I was holding up a sign!”
“It was looking at you.” Fanny was already going back to the gap. “That’s covering.”
She stole that,
thought Layla.
From the breach.
Behind her somebody was crying.
It was the small boy from the shelter doorway. He had come down the street looking for someone and found the wall instead. He stood behind her with his fists against his eyes.
Layla did not turn from the wall. She said it over her shoulder.
“If you’re scared, you can hide behind me.”
Once she had said it to Roger as a joke, and he had run across open ground for the spot behind her. She did not say it as a joke now.
The boy took a fistful of the back of her uniform and held on.
Fanny came and knelt beside him. She spoke low and soft, nothing like her command voice.
“Don’t be scared kiddo, everything’s gonna be alright.”

Layla had heard that voice once before. On the avenue, the day of the breach, Joe had knelt like that over a girl with a pink rabbit. He had spoken in a voice he never used in class. From twenty meters off, Layla had caught the voice and not the words. Then the slab came down on him, and she walked away to argue over who covered whom.
Maybe those,
she thought.
“Is she your friend?” the boy asked Layla.
Layla looked at Fanny. On her lab’s top shelf a pink box with a teal ribbon still stood beside the trophy.
“She’s my teammate.”
Fanny looked down at the stones. Her ears had gone red.

media.alt: Official art: Fanny, short orange hair and a red scarf, and Layla, long pink twin tails and a black dress, stand side by side under a blue sky, Layla grinning.

segs.t: A soldier with his arm in a sling took the boy’s hand and walked him back up the street.
For a breath nothing came over the heap. Down on the bay road the Enders were gathering again.
Fanny sat down against the tipped car and wiped her blades on her knee.
“My brother would have held this street alone,” she said, half to herself.
Layla waited.
“I don’t care what Tigreal would have done.” Fanny looked along the wall at the soldiers, then up at Layla. “I’m not doing it alone.”
She isn’t looking past me now,
thought Layla.
She sat down beside her against the car. Their shoulders touched.
In the gap Guinevere was wiping the blood off her knuckles. Layla looked down the street at the cracked stones at the mouth of the cut, where Selena had landed.
“Did she send them,” said Layla, “or did she just leave?”
Guinevere looked at the same stones. “I don’t know.”
Layla’s hand went to her ear. “The deck should hear about her.”
“Tell them what?” said Fanny. Her eyes went to Vexana. “This morning I’d have called Vexana a traitor on that channel.”
I did,
thought Layla.
At the seawall, to Guinevere’s face.
The heap shifted. Something was climbing it.
Fanny got up. Layla took her hand away from her ear.
Fanny stopped beside Guinevere in the gap.
“Don’t give up.”
“I wasn’t going to,” said Guinevere.
Two came at once this time. One came over the heap at Guinevere. The other was climbing the house front at the wall’s end, to drop down behind them.
Fanny stayed at Guinevere’s side, facing the heap. Layla came up off the stones and set her back against Fanny’s, facing up the street.
On the sand outside the dome, Fanny had done this first. Out there she had told Layla which side was hers. Since then Layla had gone first on every raid, and this morning Fanny had told her to lead.
In this street nobody went first. Fanny had the heap. Layla had the street.
The one on the house front dropped into the street behind the wall and lifted its arm.
Three,
Layla counted.
Two.
She did not say it aloud. On
now
she dropped, and her back left Fanny’s.
Fanny’s blade swept back over her own shoulder, through the air where Layla’s head had been, and into the open chest. The claw came down on the stones beside Layla’s hand.
Fanny had not looked round.
At the top of the cut, Ruby’s scythe still spat white along its edge. Oro had built it. Nothing in it ran on aspirant power, so the field had found nothing in it to put out.
The wounded lay along the house fronts below the shelters. Somewhere among them the boy was crying again.
Angela had no shield now. She was lifting a slab of fallen wall off a soldier’s legs with her bare hands. No human could have lifted it. Her body ran on her own cell, as it always had.
The man dragged himself clear. Angela set the slab down.
Fanny’s voice came on the channel. “Ruby. You’ve got the only charge left.”
Ruby looked down the street at the gap.
An Ender had climbed the house fronts past the wall. It dropped off a roof into the street behind her, straight at the soldier on the stones.
Angela threw herself over him, her back to the claw. It caught her across the back and threw her into a wall. She slid down it. Her left arm hung wrong, and sparks spat from the elbow.
Something came up in Ruby.

She knew it. It had come once before, in a burning avenue, with Angela lying still on the stones behind her. Everything had gone quiet and hot. She had cut down everything in front of her, and the lamp post behind them, and the wall. Then she had raised the scythe over a crying child.
Now the boy’s crying went far away, the way that crying had.
She had the only live blade in the street. The street was full of wounded. That rage had never cared what it hit.
In the avenue it had taken Angela’s shout to bring her back. Angela sat against the wall now with sparks at her elbow, looking up at her. Her mouth was open.
Not again,
thought Ruby.
She shouldn’t have to call me back.
She made herself hear the crying. It came near again. A small boy among the wounded.
The Ender’s claw went up over Angela. As it came down, its chest opened.
Ruby made one cut, into the core, and no more.
The Ender folded onto the stones beside Angela. Behind it a lamp post still stood. So did the wall.
Then Ruby was on her knees with both hands on Angela’s arm.
Angela was looking up at her eyes. They had stayed blue. Angela’s mouth closed.
“Ruby,” said Angela. It was not a shout.
She looked at the sparks. “It’s only the elbow,” she said. “It hurts. I know what that means.”
In the avenue she had asked how to stop it. Ruby had had no answer then.
“I made that elbow,” said Ruby. “I can mend it.”
Fanny was still waiting on the channel. The commander had put rear support with the wounded, and the wounded had nothing else.
Ruby keyed the channel.
“What I’m supposed to do, I’ll see through to the end, responsibly.”
On Oro every post had been chosen for her, inside a golden birdcage. This one she chose to keep.
Another Ender dropped into the street from the roofs. Ruby stood up between it and Angela, the scythe low.
“Don’t get in my way!”
She said it cold, and waited for it to strike.
